To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the WHO and national lists of medicines in Mexico, the Caribbean and South America are inadequate to support paediatric endocrinological and diabetes care.

1) the WHO and national Model EMLs are inadequate to promote paediatric and adult endocrinology and diabetology; 2) the national EML of the richest country in the area included medicines that were missing from the WHO EML; 3) the national ELMs could be improved by using physical maturity rather that a set age cut-off to define children, by greater standardization of the EML format, and by formatting the EML in a disease-focused way
WHO and national essential medicines lists are not adequate to promote paediatrics endocrinology and diabetology care.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the promotion of access to medicines in paediatric endocrine and diabetes care.
the availability and accessibility of medicines in paediatric endocrine diseases and diabetes in Latin America.
the availability of essential medicines in our specialty, which may help to improve the quality of paediatric endocrinological care in low and middle-income countries.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the WHO and national essential medicines lists are adequate to support the care of children with diabetes and other endocrine diseases in the countries analysed, but there are some areas for improvement.
the WHO and national lists of medicines are not yet adequate for paediatric endocrinologists and diabetologists.

the WHO and national essential medicines lists for paediatric endocrinologists and diabetologists in Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and South America, while useful, are not adequate to promote paediatrics endocrinology and diabetology care.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, while the WHO EML is largely adequate for our specialty, there is a clear need for greater standardisation of national EMLs and for a more systematic and transparent approach to updating the WHO EML.
there is room to improve both the WHO and national Model EMLs for the benefit of children in our specialty.
the WHO EML and the national EML for our region do not include all the medicines deemed necessary by paediatric endocrinologists.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the WHO and national essential medicines lists are not perfect but they are a useful starting point for the development of a list of medicines for our specialty, which can be further adapted to local needs.
the EMLs, including those from the WHO, are not adequate to promote the use of medicines for our specialty, especially in the poorest countries.
the WHO and national lists of EMLs for Mexico, the Central American and South American countries, and the Caribbean are largely adequate to promote paediatrics endocrinology and endocrinology care.
